messages.subject: Trouble with Multivariate Regression
parts:
I'm having trouble running a toy examples for multivariate regression. This stan code is:

stanMod = """
data{
    int<lower = 0> N;
    int<lower = 0> K;

    vector[K] Y[N];
    vector[N] D;

    cov_matrix[K] R;
}

parameters{
    vector[K] a;
    vector[K] b;

    cov_matrix[K] Omega;
}

transformed parameters{
    vector[K] mu[N];

    for(k in 1:K){
        for(i in 1:N){
            mu[i, k] <- a[k] + b[k] * D[i];
        }
    }
}

model{
    for(i in 1:N){
        Y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu[i], Omega);
    }

    Omega ~ inv_wishart(K+1, R);
}
"""

I get this warning:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::inv_wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): WW is not positive definite (7.3809879583185371e+71:0).
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong, if this is the right way to parameterize it. This model works in JAGS so I thought I'd try porting it over to STAN. I've read other threads that suggest the problem is in the Omega (in particular the inv_wishart coming too close to not being positive definite for the covariance matrix). I've tried numerous things, such as changing Omega from a covariance matrix to a regular matrix (relaxing the requirement of positive definiteness I think). The model runs, but the chains do not converge at all. I've tried removing the multivariate response and changing the model to:

for(i in 1:N){
        for(k in 1:K){
            Y[i, k] ~ normal(mu[i], stdev[k]);
        }
    }

I still get an error message:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is -3.364634555144618:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

but the model runs and the chains do converge. I'm not crazy about this because a) I still get error messages, b) I'm not modeling the covariance between response variables, which is preferable, and c) the parameter estimates are just too similar (almost identical) for a[1]:a[2] and b[1]:b[2], so I'm not sure I trust it.

I've tried reparameterizing to the Cholesky decomposition as in the manual, but most examples I've found are for multivariate normal of parameters, not a response, and I'm pretty sure I did it wrong.

Am I screwing something up?

We're no longer very keen on the inverse Wishart priors.
See this paper by Ben Goodrich et al.:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

But the model should still work.

>
> I get this warning:
>
> /Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:/
> /Error in function stan::prob::inv_wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): WW is not positive definite (7.3809879583185371e+71:0)./
> /If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
> sampler is fine,/
> /but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified./

For what it's worth, that's *not* an error message. We just
don't know how to make that point any clearer to users. We don't
want to get rid of it as it's helpful, but we may have to in order
to stop freaking our users out about it.

The dump of the value is a mess here --- we really need to fix
that. But that 7e71 seems to indicate that you're getting
huge values in the covariance matrix.

The key issue is: does the error persist in most iterations? If
so, there's a problem.

I think we need to lower our tolerance for positive definiteness
somehow. We're using the Eigen built-ins to do this, and they're
very picky about what counts as positive definite.

> I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong, if this is the right way to parameterize it. This model works in JAGS so I thought
> I'd try porting it over to STAN. I've read other threads that suggest the problem is in the Omega (in particular the
> inv_wishart coming too close to not being positive definite for the covariance matrix). I've tried numerous things, such
> as changing Omega from a covariance matrix to a regular matrix (relaxing the requirement of positive definiteness I
> think).

No, you need to declare Omega as a covariance matrix. In general,
the constraints on a parameter need to match its support in the model.

This error's coming from the multivariate normal distribution, not
from the parameter itself.

The model runs, but the chains do not converge at all. I've tried removing the multivariate response and
> changing the model to:
>
> for(i in 1:N){
> for(k in 1:K){
> Y[i, k] ~ normal(mu[i], stdev[k]);
> }
> }

> /If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
> sampler is fine,/

>
> but the model runs and the chains do converge. I'm not crazy about this because a) I still get error messages,
See above.

b) I'm
> not modeling the covariance between response variables, which is preferable,
Right --- this one's the deal breaker.

> and c) the parameter estimates are just too
> similar (almost identical) for a[1]:a[2] and b[1]:b[2], so I'm not sure I trust it.

I'd recommend simulating data from the model and seeing
if you can recover the parameters.

> I've tried reparameterizing to the Cholesky decomposition as in the manual, but most examples I've found are for
> multivariate normal of parameters, not a response, and I'm pretty sure I did it wrong.

You can use the Cholesky decomposition on parameters.
It's just going in as an argument to the multivariate normal.
> Am I screwing something up?

Not that I can see from the model, but I don't know what your data
are like. If the covariance really does involve terms on the scale of
7e71, there may be a problem with the data.

- Bob

We expect to get these warnings, especially with highly
constrained models. We can't seem to formulate text that
doesn't lead to these kinds of exchanges on the mailing list,
so I think it's probably best if we just get rid of them.

As warning message itself says, if they do not persist
they are not a problem. In particular they do not affect
the detailed balance of the sampler --- they are just
indicators that there's a Metropolis rejection due to
constraint violations, which is itself due to discretization
of the Hamiltonian dynamics and limited floating-point
precision.

I think the large covariances are coming from the initializations.
I saw them in the simulation, too. Even with a perfect
correlation, at convergencye, you'd only expect the posterior covariance
to be somewhere near the larger variance of the two variables.

- Bob

Bob,
I've been having this warning since transitioning to the latest version of Stan. Maybe not necessarily removing it, but having different levels of warnings displayed might be helpful (like Matlab's fmincon has a display variable that you can adjust to display increasing levels of details about an optimization).

Anyway, I had been using the following code (based on a thread from January of last year):

//For testing, I had set S_prior to the identity matrix, V_prior to S_prior times 100, and nu_prior to N.
data {
  int<lower=0> N; //# of variables
  int<lower=0> T; //# of observations
  vector[N] y[T]; //data, formatted as NxT
  vector[N] mu_prior;  //prior on mean
  cov_matrix[N] V_prior; //prior uncertainty on mean
  cov_matrix[N] S_prior; //prior on covariance
  int<lower=0> nu_prior; //prior degrees of freedom for covariance
}
transformed data {
  matrix[N, N] L_V_prior; //Haven't had any luck getting cholesky_factor_cov[N] working
  matrix[N, N] L_S_prior;
  matrix[N, N] inv_L_S_prior;
  int<lower=0> nu_post;
 
  L_V_prior <- cholesky_decompose(V_prior);
  L_S_prior <- cholesky_decompose(S_prior);
  inv_L_S_prior <- inverse(L_S_prior);
  nu_post <- T + nu_prior;
}
parameters {
  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[N, N] L_sigma;
  L_sigma <- cholesky_decompose(sigma);
}
model {
  mu ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, L_V_prior);
  sigma ~ inv_wishart(nu_post, inv_L_S_prior' * inv_L_S_prior);
  for (t in 1:T) {
    y[t] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_sigma);
  }
}

You suggest not using the inverse Wishart, but still using the Cholesky. I was able to change the end to

parameters {
  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] inv_sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[N, N] L_inv_sigma;
  L_inv_sigma <- cholesky_decompose(inv_sigma);
}
model {
  mu ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, L_V_prior);
  inv_sigma ~ wishart(nu_post, L_S_prior * L_S_prior');
  for (t in 1:T) {
    y[t] ~ multi_normal_prec(mu, L_inv_sigma * L_inv_sigma');
  }

On a separate note (not to bog you guys down with too many issues), while the extract function can allow you to only select certain outputs, my understanding is that the stan function simulates every parameter and transformed parameter (and generated quantities) from a .stan file. However, I may not always need to output all the transformed parameters (and generated quantities). In the above example, I may not really need to output the simulated stochastic volatility of each series in each point in time. As the number of variables or length of the series increases, it may cause memory issues on less powerful machines. Similarly, it might be convenient if you could input the output of a previous stan function call and then output whichever other transformed parameters or generated quantities you may need. In that example, it would be like fitting the model with one stan call and outputting only some of the parameters, then calling the stan function again to calculate the posterior predictive given the previous call. This way you wouldn't calculate the generated quantities unless you need them and you don't have to rely on separate stan files (one with generated quantities, one without) when testing.

Here are some references (the first is a more gentle introduction, the file is below the cached heading):
http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.160.8266
Nelson's "An Introduction to Copulas" is a popular reference that you could find at an academic library
http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.4204

Copulas are the multivariate dependence in a joint distribution. Sklar's theorem is the most important result, which says that any joint distribution can be expressed as some univariate distributions times the copula. The benefit of this approach is that you can model the univariate marginal distributions separately from the multivariate dependence. As such, copula estimation often requires the inverse pdf for the marginals, which might be one barrier to implementing them in Stan presently (I didn't see inverse pdfs in the manual).

I used student t marginals and a normal copula as a good example above of why copulas are helpful. Basically, if you were to instead fit a multivariate student t distribution, then you effectively assume the degrees of freedom parameter is the same across every variable. The student t + normal copula would often be fit by first fitting each of the variables with a student t distribution with each having its own degrees of freedom. Then you would create a new multivariate variable applying the appropriate student t inverse pdf to each variable. This puts each variable between 0 and 1. To fit the normal copula to this, I might apply a standard normal cdf to that and estimate the resulting correlation matrix.

Nelson's "An Introduction to Copulas" is a popular reference that you could find at an academic library
http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.4204

Copulas are the multivariate dependence in a joint distribution. Sklar's theorem is the most important result, which says that any joint distribution can be expressed as some univariate distributions times the copula. The benefit of this approach is that you can model the univariate marginal distributions separately from the multivariate dependence. As such, copula estimation often requires the inverse pdf for the marginals, which might be one barrier to implementing them in Stan presently (I didn't see inverse pdfs in the manual).

Basically, if you were to instead fit a multivariate student t distribution, then you effectively assume the degrees of freedom parameter is the same across every variable. The student t + normal copula would often be fit by first fitting each of the variables with a student t distribution with each having its own degrees of freedom. Then you would create a new multivariate variable applying the appropriate student t inverse pdf to each variable. This puts each variable between 0 and 1. To fit the normal copula to this, I might apply a standard normal cdf to that and estimate the resulting correlation matrix.

Ravi,
Just to give you a little more information. I think when I had first tried this, I didn't have much understanding of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. I still don't (compared to Gibbs Sampling), but I'm slightly more familiar with it than I used to be. The good thing about Gibbs sampling is that you can pretty much do whatever you want. Like I could throw in a PCA step to a Gibbs sampler and the only problem is that it slows everything down. You (likely) couldn't use PCA within the context of Stan because analytic formulas for PCA are ridiculous (I've tried symbolic math toolboxes for even 5x5 matrices and the formula look like just a sea of variables).

In Stan, you need to be able to provide analytic information for the log likelihood (or at least something proportional to it). The problem for a copula approach is that the copula log likelihood will have some quantile (inverse cdf) functions, depending on what the marginals are, that are not easy to calculate derivatives for. For instance, suppose you fit a t distribution to each univariate distribution. To fit the normal copula, you would then need to apply the cdf function for the relevant t to each univariate distribution and then apply the normal inverse cdf function to get normally distributed variables, which you could then estimate the correlation matrix from. Last time I checked, Stan has cdfs but not inverse cdfs, so at best you could get the uniform marginals (assuming Stan can handle taking derivatives of them, which I haven't tried). You'd then need some other approach to convert the uniform marginals to values, but even if you could write a user-defined function to do it (which you couldn't before) Stan would still need the derivatives of the functions for the HMC to work properly, I think at least.

    vector<lower=4,upper=30>[J] nu ;

parts:
1. Rather than this:

for(j in 1:J) {
for(t in 1:T)
lambda[t,j] ~ gamma(nu[j]/2,nu[j]/2) ;

you can use:
for (t in 1:T)

lambda[t] ~ gamma(nu / 2, nu / 2);

Even better would be to not divide nu by 2 twice, but to do it once
and assign it to a temporary.

2. Replace
for (t in 1:T) {

for (j in 1:J)
lambdainvsqrt[t][j] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[t][j]) ;
LSigma[t] <- LRho * diag_matrix(sigma) * diag_matrix(lambdainvsqrt[t]) ;
}

with

{
matrix[J,J] LRho_times_diag_matrix_sigma;
LRho_sigma <- diag_post_multiply(LRho, sigma);
for (t in 1:T) {

for (j in 1:J)
lambdainvsqrt[t][j] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[t][j]) ;
LSigma[t] <- diag_post_multiply(LRho_sigma, lambda_inv_sqrt[t]);
}

It may be even faster in a loop due to the sparsity. In just
two dimensions, you can just write

LSigma[t,1,1] <- ...
LSigma[t,2,2] <- ...
LSigma[t,2,1] <- ...
LSigma[t,1,2] <- 0; // lower triangular

with ... replaced by the reuslt of all the above matrix multiplication.
Make sure to save intermediate computations.

3. If you don't need to save lambda_inv_sqrt[t], make it a local in the
same scope.



4. This isn't a speed issue per se, but Andrew's been very down on the constrained
uniform priors (though we still have some in our manual):
vector<lower=0,upper=100>[J] sigma ; // scale of multivariate vector

vector<lower=2,upper=30>[J] nu ; // degrees of freedom of multivariate vector

Rather than this, you can just put a real prior on sigma and nu and leave
them unconstrained (well, they need lower=0 at least).

5. Given that you only have a two-dimensional Cholesky factor, you could
just parameterize directly on the correlation rho.

- Bob
